title: Round-Robin Scheduling: Fairness by the Slice
topic: Round-robin scheduling — give every ready job one fixed-length time slice in turn; short jobs respond fast, long jobs make steady progress

beats.narration: Three programs are ready to run, but only one CPU. Who goes first — and for how long?

elements.content: Three jobs, one CPU — whose turn is it?

beats.narration: First in, first out runs each job to completion. Job A is long, so jobs B and C wait — and a quick keystroke in C can sit idle for seconds. That is starvation by queue order.

elements.content: Gantt timeline with A taking the first eight units, then B for two, then C for two
C's average response time = 10 — the user waits forever

beats.narration: Round-robin fixes that. Pick a fixed time slice — say one unit — give it to the next ready job, then rotate. The queue keeps spinning while everyone makes progress.

elements.content: Circular ready queue with three jobs A, B, C; an arrow rotates around the queue
every tick: head of the queue runs for q, then goes to the back

beats.narration: Watch the Gantt chart fill up. A, B, C, A, B, C — every job gets the CPU within one tick of being ready. Response time becomes predictable.

elements.content: Gantt chart that fills cell by cell as the playhead sweeps from left to right; cells coloured by job
Sweeping playhead synced to the rotation of the queue above

beats.narration: A small slice feels snappy but spends time on context switches. A big slice runs efficiently but starts to look like FIFO. Picking the slice is the whole game.

elements.content: responsive, but switches eat the CPU
efficient, but jobs at the back wait
pick q just long enough to amortize the switch
